summary: Year-1 children move from comparing lengths to quantifying them: laying identical units (cubes, paper clips) end to end, counting them with no gaps or overlaps, and then beginning to read a centimetre ruler. The core concept is that a measurement is a count of equal-sized length-units tiling the object completely, always recorded as a number WITH a unit.
misconceptions: Leaves gaps between units or overlaps them, treating measuring as 'placing things along' rather than covering the length.
Uses mixed-size units yet counts them as one total.
Counts the number of discrete objects (cardinality) rather than the length covered — e.g. a row of 6 short matches is called 'longer' than an equal row of 5 longer matches.
Begins counting the ruler at the numeral '1' instead of the zero/start.

activities.title: Tile the length with identical cubes
steps: Place a pencil or book in front of you and a tub of same-size cubes beside it.
Lay cube after cube along the pencil, end to end, from one end of the pencil.
Nudge the cubes so each one touches the next with no gaps and no overlaps.
Count the cubes and say the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes'.
Run a finger along the pencil to check no uncovered stretch is left between cubes.
activities.insight: A length-count only means the length when identical units cover the object completely, with no gaps and no overlaps.

activities.title: Why the units must all be the same size
steps: Measure the book again, but this time use a bin that has a few oversized blocks mixed in with the small cubes.
Report the total and check whether it makes sense.
Try the challenge: '3 large blocks and 4 small blocks laid in a row — is the book 7 blocks long?' Explain your answer.
Re-measure the book using only one size of unit and compare.
activities.insight: A measurement is only meaningful when every unit is the same size; mixing sizes makes the count nonsense.

activities.title: Length is extent, not how many pieces
steps: Look at two rows of matches: one row made of 6 short matches and one row made of 5 longer matches.
Decide which row is longer, or whether they are the same length, and say what you are counting.
Lay the two rows directly side by side, aligned at one end, to check your answer.
activities.insight: Length is how far something extends, not how many pieces make up the row; more pieces does not mean longer.

activities.title: Build a paper ruler and read a centimetre ruler
steps: Take a strip of paper and mark off one chosen unit over and over, end to end, to make your own ruler.
Use your paper ruler to measure a short object, counting the units.
Now take a centimetre ruler and line its start (the 0) up with one end of the object, not the '1' mark.
Read off how many centimetres long the object is and record it as a number with its unit, e.g. '15 cm'.
activities.insight: A ruler is just a tool that counts the same iterated units; you start from zero because the numerals name the units of space already covered.

activities.title: Spot-the-gap and how-many checks
steps: Look at several pictured rows and pick which one has been measured correctly (no gaps, no overlaps, equal units).
For a tidy row of cubes, say or set a slider to how many cubes long it is.
For a ruler picture, say how many centimetres long the object is.
activities.insight: You can recognise a correctly measured row and read a count, but recognising one does not by itself build the skill of producing a clean row yourself.

checkQuestion: Set out a book, a tub of same-size cubes with a few larger blocks mixed in, and a centimetre ruler. Say: 'Measure how long this book is and tell me the number.' Do not tell them how. Watch how they lay the units, whether they mix sizes, and where they start the ruler; then ask them to write the result down.
checkAnswer: The child lays identical units end to end from one end of the book with no gaps or overlaps, counts the length-units (not the objects at random), states and records the count WITH a unit ('about 12 cubes' / '15 cm'), and — when they reach for the ruler — aligns its start (0) with the end of the book rather than the '1' mark.
